# The question

Every winter the air in Yerevan becomes unhealthy. The official explanation is
geography and climate: the city sits in a basin, and in the cold months a layer
of still air (a temperature inversion) acts like a lid that traps pollution.

If weather is the whole story, there is little the city can do. If the
pollution is produced by people and only trapped by the weather, there is room
for policy. So we ask:

> **How much of Yerevan's winter PM2.5 pollution is explained by weather, and
> how much by human activity?**

**Our hypothesis:** weather decides *how much* pollution stays over the city,
but people decide *whether there is anything to trap*.

PM2.5 means particles smaller than 2.5 micrometres. They are small enough to
reach deep into the lungs, which is why the World Health Organization (WHO) sets
a guideline of **15 µg/m³ for a 24-hour average**.

# Data and preparation

```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)   # data wrangling and ggplot2
library(lubridate)   # dates and time zones
library(patchwork)   # combining plots
library(broom)       # tidy model output
library(sandwich)    # robust (Newey-West) standard errors
library(lmtest)      # coefficient tests with robust errors
library(ggrepel)     # non-overlapping labels
library(scales)      # axis labels
```

We use three main files, and two small files of published figures that are
used only in Section 8:

| File | Content | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `yerevan_pm_hourly_sensorcommunity_full.csv` | Hourly PM2.5 and PM10 per sensor | Sensor.community (citizen sensors) |
| `yerevan_pm_sensors_full.csv` | Sensor type and coordinates | Sensor.community |
| `yerevan_weather_hourly_openmeteo_2023_2026.csv` | Hourly weather for central Yerevan | Open-Meteo (ERA5 reanalysis) |
| `armenia_household_gas_monthly_2020.csv` | Natural gas used by households, by month | R2E2 (2022), Figure 1.5 |
| `yerevan_heating_fuels.csv` | Heating fuels of Yerevan households and PM2.5 emitted per unit of heat | ILCS 2020 survey in R2E2 (2022); German emission inventory (2025) |

## Settings

All thresholds are defined once here, so every later step uses the same values
and a change needs to be made in one place only.

```{r settings}
data_dir <- "data"                     # folder that contains the data files

EXCLUDED_SENSORS <- c(83835, 99632)    # see "Cleaning" below
MIN_READINGS     <- 5                  # raw readings needed for a valid hour
MIN_HOURS        <- 18                 # valid hours needed for a valid day (75%)
WHO_DAILY        <- 15                 # WHO 24-hour PM2.5 guideline, µg/m³
WINTER_MONTHS    <- c(11, 12, 1, 2)    # heating season
EPISODE_LEVEL    <- 25                 # WHO interim target 2 (24-hour), used to define an episode
CALM_WIND        <- 1.4                # m/s: the median winter daily wind, our line for "still air"
WARM_MONTHS      <- 5:9                # no heating
HUMID_LIMIT      <- 90                 # relative humidity (%) used in robustness
HOLIDAYS         <- c("12-31", "01-01", "01-02", "01-03", "01-04",
                      "01-05", "01-06", "01-07")   # official non-working days in Armenia
PANEL_SENSORS    <- c(80868, 83131, 84847, 85218)  # sensors active in all winters
LONG_SENSORS     <- c(80868, 83131)    # sensors covering all three winters fully
LOCAL_TZ         <- "Asia/Yerevan"     # UTC+4, no daylight saving
```

## Loading

Column types are stated explicitly, so R never has to guess them.

```{r load}
read_project_csv <- function(file, col_types) {
  path <- file.path(data_dir, file)
  if (!file.exists(path)) stop("File not found: ", path)
  read_csv(path, col_types = col_types)
}

pm_raw <- read_project_csv(
  "yerevan_pm_hourly_sensorcommunity_full.csv",
  cols(sensor_id = col_integer(), hour_utc = col_datetime(),
       pm10 = col_double(), pm25 = col_double(),
       n_readings_pm10 = col_integer(), n_readings_pm25 = col_integer())
)
sensors <- read_project_csv(
  "yerevan_pm_sensors_full.csv",
  cols(sensor_id = col_integer(), sensor_type = col_character(),
       lat = col_double(), lon = col_double())
)
weather_raw <- read_project_csv(
  "yerevan_weather_hourly_openmeteo_2023_2026.csv",
  cols(time = col_datetime(), .default = col_double())
)
```

## Integrity checks

Before any analysis we confirm the data is what we think it is. If any check
fails, the report stops here.

```{r checks}
stopifnot(
  "duplicate sensor-hour rows" = !any(duplicated(pm_raw[c("sensor_id", "hour_utc")])),
  "negative PM values"         = all(pm_raw$pm25 >= 0 & pm_raw$pm10 >= 0),
  "PM2.5 larger than PM10"     = all(pm_raw$pm25 <= pm_raw$pm10),
  "gaps in weather series"     = all(diff(as.numeric(weather_raw$time)) == 3600)
)

tibble(
  Table  = c("PM (sensor-hours)", "Sensors", "Weather (hours)"),
  Rows   = c(nrow(pm_raw), nrow(sensors), nrow(weather_raw)),
  `Missing values` = c(sum(is.na(pm_raw)), sum(is.na(sensors)), sum(is.na(weather_raw)))
)
```

The only missing values are in the weather file, all in `boundary_layer_height`
(January to June 2024). We keep those rows and remove them explicitly, with
`filter(!is.na(...))`, only in the steps that need this variable.

## Cleaning

```{r clean}
pm <- pm_raw %>%
  filter(!sensor_id %in% EXCLUDED_SENSORS,     # keep the comparable Yerevan sensors
         n_readings_pm25 >= MIN_READINGS) %>%  # keep hours with enough raw readings
  select(sensor_id, hour_utc, pm25, pm10)

weather <- weather_raw %>%
  transmute(
    hour_utc = time,
    temp = temperature_2m,            # °C
    rh   = relative_humidity_2m,      # %
    rain = precipitation,             # mm
    wind = wind_speed_10m,            # m/s
    blh  = boundary_layer_height      # m
  )
```

- **Excluded sensors.** Sensor 83835 is not located in Yerevan. Sensor 99632 is
  a different sensor model that only started in June 2026, has no winter data,
  and reads about three times higher than the others. Keeping it would distort
  the city value.
- **Minimum readings.** A sensor reports about every 2.5 minutes. An hour built
  from fewer than `r MIN_READINGS` readings is not a reliable hourly average.
  This removes `r percent(mean(pm_raw$n_readings_pm25 < MIN_READINGS), 0.1)` of rows.

After cleaning we have `r comma(nrow(pm))` sensor-hours from
`r n_distinct(pm$sensor_id)` sensors.

**Boundary layer height (BLH)** is the key weather variable in this report. It
is the height of the layer of air next to the ground in which pollution can
mix. A low value means a low "lid" over the city.

## City index, local time and seasons

The timestamps are in UTC. People live on local time, so we convert **before**
any hour-of-day or weekday analysis.

For each hour we take the **median** across sensors as the city value. The
median is not affected by one faulty or badly placed sensor.

```{r city-index}
add_time_parts <- function(data) {
  data %>%
    mutate(
      local_time = with_tz(hour_utc, LOCAL_TZ),
      date    = as_date(local_time),
      hour    = hour(local_time),
      month   = month(local_time),
      weekday = factor(c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")[wday(local_time, week_start = 1)],
                       levels = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")),
      season  = case_when(month %in% WINTER_MONTHS ~ "Winter",
                          month %in% WARM_MONTHS   ~ "Warm season",
                          TRUE                     ~ "Transition")
    )
}

build_city_hourly <- function(pm_data) {
  pm_data %>%
    group_by(hour_utc) %>%
    summarise(pm25 = median(pm25), pm10 = median(pm10), n_sensors = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
    left_join(weather, by = "hour_utc") %>%   # keep every PM hour, even without weather
    add_time_parts()
}

city_hourly <- build_city_hourly(pm)
```

`left_join()` keeps all `r comma(nrow(city_hourly))` city hours. The weather
file ends one day earlier than the PM file, so
`r sum(is.na(city_hourly$temp))` hours have no weather. They are used in the
descriptive charts and drop out only where weather is needed.

## Daily table

The WHO guideline refers to a 24-hour average, so we need daily values. A day
counts only if it has at least `r MIN_HOURS` valid hours (75%). A "daily mean"
built from a few night hours would not be comparable.

```{r daily}
weather_daily <- weather %>%
  mutate(date = as_date(with_tz(hour_utc, LOCAL_TZ))) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(temp = mean(temp), rh = mean(rh), wind = mean(wind),
            blh = mean(blh), rain_mm = sum(rain), rain_day = sum(rain) > 0, .groups = "drop")

winter_label <- function(date) {
  start_year <- if_else(month(date) >= 11, year(date), year(date) - 1)
  paste0(start_year, "/", str_sub(start_year + 1, 3, 4))
}

build_daily <- function(hourly) {
  hourly %>%
    group_by(date) %>%
    summarise(pm25 = mean(pm25), n_hours = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
    filter(n_hours >= MIN_HOURS) %>%
    left_join(weather_daily, by = "date") %>%
    mutate(month   = month(date),
           is_weekend = wday(date, week_start = 1) >= 6,
           season  = case_when(month %in% WINTER_MONTHS ~ "Winter",
                               month %in% WARM_MONTHS   ~ "Warm season",
                               TRUE                     ~ "Transition"),
           winter  = if_else(season == "Winter", winter_label(date), NA_character_))
}

city_daily   <- build_daily(city_hourly)
winter_daily <- city_daily %>% filter(season == "Winter")
```

We have `r nrow(city_daily)` valid days, of which `r nrow(winter_daily)` are
winter days (November to February).

## Visual style

One theme and one colour vocabulary are used in every chart:

- **Winter is always dark blue, the warm season always orange.** The two differ
  in hue and in lightness, so they stay distinguishable for colour-blind
  readers and in greyscale (Okabe-Ito palette).
- **The WHO guideline is always the same red dashed line.**
- **Amounts of pollution** use a sequential palette where darker means more.
- Titles state the finding; subtitles say what is plotted.

The rules behind these choices come from the course. **Tufte's principles**: the
visual size of an effect must match its size in the data (Lie Factor near 1), so
bars start at zero and no chart is drawn in 3D; everything carries units and a
source (thorough labelling); and every comparison is shown against something
(*"compared to what?"*). **Data-ink**: anything that can be erased without losing
information is removed. **Gestalt principles** group elements on purpose:
enclosure (shaded winter bands), proximity (panels and paired bars), connection
(lines over points), similarity (one colour per season everywhere).
**Colour** follows the HCL logic: a qualitative pair for seasons, sequential
scales for amounts, diverging scales centred on zero for residuals and
correlations. 

```{r style}
COL_WINTER <- "#0B4F8A"
COL_WARM   <- "#E69F00"
COL_WHO    <- "#C0392B"
COL_GREY   <- "grey45"
SEASON_COLOURS <- c("Winter" = COL_WINTER, "Warm season" = COL_WARM)
PM_AXIS     <- "PM2.5 (\u00b5g/m\u00b3)"              # unicode escapes: safe on any computer
PM_AXIS_LOG <- "PM2.5 (\u00b5g/m\u00b3, log scale)"
PM_LEGEND   <- "Median PM2.5\n(\u00b5g/m\u00b3)"
SOURCE <- "Data: Sensor.community (PM2.5), Open-Meteo / ERA5 (weather). Local time (UTC+4)."

theme_project <- function(base_size = 12) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = base_size + 2),
      plot.subtitle      = element_text(colour = "grey30", margin = margin(b = 10)),
      plot.caption       = element_text(colour = "grey45", size = base_size - 3, hjust = 0),
      plot.title.position   = "plot",
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
      legend.position    = "top",
      legend.justification = "left",
      strip.text         = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0)
    )
}
theme_set(theme_project())

who_line <- function() {
  geom_hline(yintercept = WHO_DAILY, colour = COL_WHO, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6)
}
```

# How bad is it, and when?

## Three years of daily air quality

```{r fig-timeline, fig.height=4.6}
winter_spans <- winter_daily %>%
  group_by(winter) %>%
  summarise(start = min(date), end = max(date), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(city_daily, aes(date, pm25)) +
  geom_rect(data = winter_spans, inherit.aes = FALSE,
            aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            fill = COL_WINTER, alpha = 0.10) +
  geom_text(data = winter_spans, inherit.aes = FALSE,
            aes(x = start + (end - start) / 2, y = 108, label = paste("Winter", winter)),
            colour = COL_WINTER, size = 3.3, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_line(colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.35) +
  who_line() +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2024-08-15"), y = WHO_DAILY, vjust = -0.8,
           label = "WHO guideline: 15", colour = COL_WHO, size = 3.3) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y", expand = expansion(0.01)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 112), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.02))) +
  labs(title = "Every winter, Yerevan's air rises far above the WHO guideline",
       subtitle = "Daily mean PM2.5, median of the city's sensors. Shaded bands are November to February.",
       x = NULL, y = PM_AXIS, caption = SOURCE)
```

```{r exceedance-numbers}
exceed_winter <- mean(winter_daily$pm25 > WHO_DAILY)
exceed_warm   <- mean(city_daily$pm25[city_daily$season == "Warm season"] > WHO_DAILY)
```

A line chart is the natural choice for a continuous time series: the line shows
the order and the connection between days. The shaded bands group the winter
days (Gestalt principle of enclosure), and the WHO line gives the "compared to
what?" context. The y-axis starts at zero so the height above the guideline is
not exaggerated.

**What we see.** The pattern repeats each year: clean from spring to autumn,
then a wall of pollution from November. In winter,
**`r percent(exceed_winter)` of days exceed the WHO guideline**; in the warm
season, `r percent(exceed_warm, 0.1)`.

## A calendar of bad days

```{r fig-calendar, fig.height=6.2}
who_breaks <- c(0, 15, 25, 37.5, 50, 75, Inf)
who_labels <- c("up to 15 (within guideline)", "15 to 25", "25 to 37.5", "37.5 to 50", "50 to 75", "above 75")

city_daily %>%
  mutate(level = cut(pm25, who_breaks, who_labels),
         year  = year(date),
         month_name = factor(month.abb[month], levels = rev(month.abb))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(day(date), month_name, fill = level)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ year, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "rocket", direction = -1, drop = FALSE,
                       name = "Daily PM2.5 (\u00b5g/m\u00b3)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 10, 20, 31), expand = expansion(0)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "Bad air is a season, not an accident",
       subtitle = "Each tile is one day. Empty tiles are days without enough data.",
       x = "Day of month", y = NULL, caption = SOURCE) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "right",
        panel.spacing = unit(1.2, "lines"))
```

A heatmap shows every single day without overplotting. The classes are the
WHO guideline (15) and the WHO interim targets (25, 37.5, 50, 75), so each
colour step has a health meaning. The palette is sequential (light to dark)
because the data runs from low to high, and it is colour-blind safe.

**What we see.** The dark tiles form the same block every year, from November
to February. Inside the block there are also light days: winter air is not
bad *every* day. Section 5 asks what separates the dark days from the light
ones.

## The seasonal gap

```{r fig-monthly, fig.height=4.8}
monthly <- city_daily %>%
  mutate(month_name = factor(month.abb[month], levels = month.abb),
         period = if_else(season == "Winter", "Winter", "Rest of the year"))

monthly_share <- monthly %>%
  group_by(month_name) %>%
  summarise(share = mean(pm25 > WHO_DAILY), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(monthly, aes(month_name, pm25)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = period), outlier.size = 0.7, outlier.alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.35) +
  who_line() +
  geom_text(data = monthly_share, aes(y = 190, label = percent(share, 1)),
            size = 3.2, colour = "grey25") +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(1, 2, 5, 15, 50, 100)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Winter" = COL_WINTER, "Rest of the year" = "grey80"), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.4, 12.6), expand = FALSE, ylim = c(0.8, 230)) +
  labs(title = "December air is about nine times dirtier than May air",
       subtitle = "Distribution of daily PM2.5 by month, all years (log scale).\nNumbers on top: share of days above the WHO guideline.",
       x = NULL, y = PM_AXIS_LOG, caption = SOURCE)
```

```{r monthly-numbers}
month_median <- city_hourly %>% group_by(month) %>% summarise(med = median(pm25))
dec_med <- month_median$med[month_median$month == 12]
may_med <- month_median$med[month_median$month == 5]
```

Boxplots compare whole distributions, not only averages. PM2.5 is strongly
right-skewed (most days are low, a few are very high), so we use a log scale.
On a linear scale the summer boxes would be squeezed flat.

**What we see.** The median hour in December is `r round(dec_med, 1)` µg/m³,
against `r round(may_med, 1)` in May: a factor of
`r round(dec_med / may_med, 1)`. From April to October almost no day exceeds
the guideline.

# Can we trust citizen sensors?

The sensors are low-cost devices run by volunteers. If they measure something
real, sensors in different parts of the city should rise and fall together.

```{r fig-correlation, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=5.2}
sensor_daily <- pm %>%
  mutate(date = as_date(with_tz(hour_utc, LOCAL_TZ))) %>%
  group_by(sensor_id, date) %>%
  summarise(pm25 = mean(pm25), n_hours = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n_hours >= MIN_HOURS)

cor_matrix <- sensor_daily %>%
  select(sensor_id, date, pm25) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = sensor_id, values_from = pm25) %>%
  select(-date) %>%
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs")   # each pair uses the days both sensors have

cor_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_matrix)) %>%
  rename(sensor_a = Var1, sensor_b = Var2, r = Freq) %>%
  filter(as.integer(sensor_a) > as.integer(sensor_b))   # lower triangle only

ggplot(cor_long, aes(sensor_b, sensor_a, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r)), colour = "white", size = 3.6) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, limits = c(0, 1), name = "Correlation") +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(title = "The sensors tell the same story",
       subtitle = "Correlation of daily PM2.5 between each pair of sensors",
       x = "Sensor", y = "Sensor", caption = SOURCE) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "right")
```

A correlation matrix is symmetric, so we show only the lower triangle: the
other half would repeat the same numbers. The colour scale runs over the full
0 to 1 range, so high values are not visually exaggerated.

**What we see.** All pairs correlate between `r sprintf("%.2f", min(cor_long$r))`
and `r sprintf("%.2f", max(cor_long$r))`. Independent devices in different
districts agree almost perfectly, so the signal is real and city-wide.

# The weather effect

## The lid over the city

```{r model-data}
# Winter days that have boundary layer data
winter_model_data <- winter_daily %>% filter(!is.na(blh))
```

```{r fig-blh, fig.height=4.8}
winter_model_data %>%
  mutate(wind_class = if_else(wind < median(wind), "Calmer half of days", "Windier half of days")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(blh, pm25)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = wind_class), alpha = 0.7, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black", linewidth = 0.7, fill = "grey75") +
  who_line() +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Calmer half of days" = "#7B3294", "Windier half of days" = "#35978F"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "The lower the lid, the dirtier the air",
       subtitle = "Winter days: daily PM2.5 against daily mean boundary layer height. Both axes on log scale.",
       x = "Boundary layer height (m, log scale)", y = PM_AXIS_LOG, caption = SOURCE)
```

A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numeric variables. On log
scales the relationship is close to a straight line, which is why we later
model `log(PM2.5)`. The grey band is the 95% confidence interval of the fitted
line.

**What we see.** Days with a boundary layer below 50 m are mostly far above the
guideline; days above 300 m are mostly below it. Calm days (purple) sit higher
than windy days (green) at the same lid height.

## Lid and wind together

```{r fig-weather-grid, fig.height=4.2}
winter_hours <- city_hourly %>% filter(season == "Winter", !is.na(blh))

winter_hours %>%
  mutate(blh_class  = cut(blh, c(0, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, Inf),
                          c("under 25", "25-50", "50-100", "100-200", "200-400", "400-800", "over 800")),
         wind_class = cut(wind, c(-Inf, 1, 2, 3, Inf),
                          c("under 1", "1-2", "2-3", "over 3"))) %>%
  group_by(blh_class, wind_class) %>%
  summarise(pm25 = median(pm25), n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n >= 30) %>%                       # medians of tiny groups are not reliable
  ggplot(aes(blh_class, wind_class, fill = pm25)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(pm25), colour = pm25 > 20), size = 3.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "rocket", direction = -1, limits = c(0, NA), name = PM_LEGEND) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "white", "FALSE" = "black")) +
  labs(title = "Winter air is clean only with strong wind or a very high lid",
       subtitle = "Median PM2.5 of winter hours for each combination of lid height and wind speed (groups of 30+ hours).",
       x = "Boundary layer height (m)", y = "Wind speed (m/s)", caption = SOURCE) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "right")
```

With thousands of hours a scatterplot would be one dark cloud (overplotting),
so we bin both variables and show the median of each cell.

**What we see.** The darkest cells are in the bottom row: when the air is
still, pollution stays high even under a moderately high lid. The air becomes
clean only when the wind is strong or the lid rises above about 800 m.

## How much of winter does weather explain?

We fit a linear model on the `r nrow(winter_model_data)` winter days:

$$\log(\text{PM2.5}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log(\text{BLH}) + \beta_2\,\text{wind} + \beta_3\,\text{temperature} + \beta_4\,\text{humidity} + \beta_5\,\text{rain} + \varepsilon$$

We model the logarithm because PM2.5 is right-skewed and weather acts
multiplicatively (it dilutes pollution by a factor, not by a fixed amount).
Pollution on one day is related to the day before, so ordinary standard errors
would be too optimistic. We use Newey-West standard errors, which correct for
this.

```{r weather-model}
weather_model <- lm(log(pm25) ~ log(blh) + wind + temp + rh + rain_day, data = winter_model_data)
weather_r2    <- summary(weather_model)$r.squared

robust <- coeftest(weather_model, vcov. = NeweyWest(weather_model))

# Turn log-coefficients into "% change in PM2.5" for an easy-to-read step in each variable
effects <- tibble(
  term  = rownames(robust)[-1],
  beta  = robust[-1, "Estimate"],
  se    = robust[-1, "Std. Error"],
  step  = c(log(2), 1, 5, 10, 1),
  label = c("Boundary layer twice as high", "Wind +1 m/s", "Temperature +5 \u00b0C",
            "Humidity +10 points", "Day with rain or snow")
) %>%
  mutate(effect = exp(beta * step) - 1,
         low    = exp((beta - 1.96 * se) * step) - 1,
         high   = exp((beta + 1.96 * se) * step) - 1,
         clear  = low > 0 | high < 0)
```

```{r fig-coefficients, fig.height=3.6}
ggplot(effects, aes(effect, reorder(label, -effect), colour = clear)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = low, xmax = high), linewidth = 0.8, size = 0.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = COL_WINTER, "FALSE" = "grey60"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "A higher lid and more wind clean the air; the other variables show no clear effect",
       subtitle = "Change in winter daily PM2.5 for a step in each weather variable, others held fixed.\nBars are 95% confidence intervals; grey means the interval includes zero.",
       x = "Change in PM2.5", y = NULL, caption = SOURCE)
```

A coefficient plot shows the size of each effect together with its
uncertainty. An interval that crosses zero means the data cannot tell the
effect apart from no effect.

**What we see.** Doubling the boundary layer height lowers PM2.5 by
`r percent(-effects$effect[1])`, and each extra m/s of wind by
`r percent(-effects$effect[2])`. Together, the weather variables explain
**`r percent(weather_r2)` of the day-to-day variation** in winter PM2.5.

```{r fig-predicted, fig.height=5.2}
winter_model_data %>%
  mutate(predicted = exp(fitted(weather_model))) %>%
  select(date, winter, Measured = pm25, `Predicted from weather alone` = predicted) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(Measured, `Predicted from weather alone`), names_to = "series", values_to = "pm25") %>%
  filter(winter != "2023/24") %>%          # 2023/24 has boundary layer data for Nov-Dec only
  ggplot(aes(date, pm25, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ paste("Winter", winter), scales = "free_x", ncol = 1) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Measured" = "grey15", "Predicted from weather alone" = "#D55E00"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Weather tells us which winter days will be bad",
       subtitle = "Measured daily PM2.5 and the value predicted by the weather model.",
       x = NULL, y = PM_AXIS_LOG, caption = SOURCE)
```

**What we see.** The predicted line follows the main episodes and the clean
breaks between them. So the official explanation is partly right: **weather
decides which days are bad.** But this only describes variation *within*
winter. It does not yet say why there is something to trap. For that we
compare winter with the warm season.

# How episodes build and break

Winter pollution does not arrive one day and leave the next. It accumulates.
This section finishes the weather side of the story: weather sets not only the
level of a single day, but how pollution stacks up over many days.

```{r episode-data}
winter_series <- winter_daily %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(winter) %>%
  mutate(
    change   = c(NA, diff(log(pm25))),   # day-to-day change, in log terms = relative change
    is_calm  = !is.na(wind) & wind < CALM_WIND,
    calm_run = sequence(rle(is_calm)$lengths) * is_calm   # length of the current calm streak
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Episodes = runs of consecutive winter days above the WHO interim target
episode_runs <- winter_series %>%
  group_by(winter) %>%
  summarise(runs = list(rle(pm25 > EPISODE_LEVEL)), .groups = "drop")

episode_lengths <- episode_runs$runs %>% map(~ .x$lengths[.x$values]) %>% unlist()

# Correlation between a day and the day before it, using only real consecutive pairs
persistence <- winter_series %>%
  group_by(winter) %>%
  mutate(previous = if_else(date - lag(date) == 1, lag(pm25), NA_real_)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  summarise(r = cor(pm25, previous, use = "complete.obs")) %>%
  pull(r)
```

```{r fig-accumulation, fig.height=4.2}
calm_build <- winter_series %>%
  filter(is_calm, calm_run >= 1) %>%
  mutate(run = pmin(calm_run, 5)) %>%
  group_by(run) %>%
  summarise(pm25 = median(pm25), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

wind_change <- winter_series %>%
  filter(!is.na(change)) %>%
  mutate(wind_class = cut(wind, quantile(wind, c(0, .25, .5, .75, 1), na.rm = TRUE),
                          include.lowest = TRUE,
                          labels = c("Calmest\nquarter", "2nd", "3rd", "Windiest\nquarter"))) %>%
  group_by(wind_class) %>%
  summarise(pct_per_day = exp(mean(change)) - 1, n = n(), .groups = "drop")

p_build <- ggplot(calm_build, aes(factor(run), pm25)) +
  geom_col(fill = COL_WINTER, width = 0.7) +
  who_line() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(pm25)), vjust = -0.5, size = 3.6, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5 or more")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(subtitle = "Each still day adds to the last",
       x = "Consecutive days with light wind", y = PM_AXIS)

p_clear <- ggplot(wind_change, aes(wind_class, pct_per_day, fill = pct_per_day > 0)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(pct_per_day, 1), vjust = if_else(pct_per_day > 0, -0.5, 1.4)),
            size = 3.6, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(), expand = expansion(0.18)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = COL_WHO, "FALSE" = "#35978F"), guide = "none") +
  labs(subtitle = "Wind undoes it",
       x = "Winter days sorted by wind speed", y = "Change from one day to the next")

p_build + p_clear +
  plot_annotation(title = "Pollution piles up on still days and is swept out by wind",
                  caption = SOURCE)
```

The left panel starts at zero because bar length is the comparison (Tufte's
first principle). The right panel is a change, so it is drawn around a zero
line, and the two directions are coloured differently.

**What we see.** "Still" here means a daily mean wind below `r CALM_WIND` m/s,
the middle of our winter days. After one still day the city sits at
`r round(calm_build$pm25[1])` µg/m³; after five it is
`r round(calm_build$pm25[nrow(calm_build)])`. In the calmest quarter of days
pollution grows by `r percent(wind_change$pct_per_day[1], 1)` per day, while in
the windiest quarter it falls by
`r percent(abs(wind_change$pct_per_day[nrow(wind_change)]), 1)`. One winter day
is strongly related to the one before it (correlation
`r sprintf("%.2f", persistence)`), which is why episodes last:
`r length(episode_lengths)` of them in three winters, lasting
`r median(episode_lengths)` days at the middle and up to
`r max(episode_lengths)`, and together covering
`r percent(sum(episode_lengths) / nrow(winter_series))` of all winter days.

## The longest episode

```{r fig-episode, fig.height=5.4}
longest <- winter_series %>%
  group_by(winter) %>%
  mutate(block = cumsum(pm25 <= EPISODE_LEVEL | is.na(pm25))) %>%
  filter(pm25 > EPISODE_LEVEL) %>%
  group_by(winter, block) %>%
  filter(n() == max(episode_lengths)) %>%
  ungroup()

window <- winter_series %>%
  filter(date >= min(longest$date) - 4, date <= max(longest$date) + 4)

band <- annotate("rect", xmin = min(longest$date) - 0.5, xmax = max(longest$date) + 0.5,
                 ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = COL_WINTER, alpha = 0.10)

p_ep_pm <- ggplot(window, aes(date, pm25)) +
  band +
  geom_line(colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.6) + geom_point(size = 1.6, colour = "grey20") +
  who_line() +
  annotate("text", x = min(longest$date), y = max(window$pm25) * 1.02,
           label = paste(max(episode_lengths), "days in a row above", EPISODE_LEVEL),
           hjust = 0, fontface = "bold", colour = COL_WINTER, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(subtitle = "Daily PM2.5", x = NULL, y = PM_AXIS)

p_ep_wx <- window %>%
  select(date, `Boundary layer (m)` = blh, `Wind (m/s)` = wind, `Rain or snow (mm)` = rain_mm) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date) %>%
  mutate(name = fct_inorder(name)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(date, value)) +
  band +
  geom_line(colour = COL_GREY, linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ name, ncol = 3, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(subtitle = "The weather over the same days", x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = SOURCE)

p_ep_pm / p_ep_wx + plot_layout(heights = c(2, 1.3))
```

The weather panels share the x-axis with the pollution panel, so each day can
be read straight down (Gestalt principle of proximity and alignment).

```{r episode-numbers}
ep_start <- min(longest$date); ep_end <- max(longest$date)
```

**What we see.** From `r format(ep_start, "%d %B")` to
`r format(ep_end, "%d %B %Y")` the city stayed above the WHO interim target for
`r max(episode_lengths)` days in a row. The wind never rose, the lid sank from
about `r round(longest$blh[1])` m to `r round(min(longest$blh))` m, and
pollution climbed from `r round(longest$pm25[1])` to
`r round(max(longest$pm25))` µg/m³. What ended it was
`r round(sum(window$rain_mm[window$date >= ep_end - 2 & window$date <= ep_end + 2], na.rm = TRUE), 1)` mm
of precipitation and a higher lid.

The relief did not last. Within a few days the level was climbing again,
because nothing had changed on the ground: rain and wind remove what is already
in the air, not what produces it.

Nothing here says anything about sources yet. It says that the city emits
steadily, and that the weather decides whether those emissions disperse or
accumulate. The next section asks what happens when the same weather meets a
city that is not heating.

# Same weather, different air

If weather alone created the pollution, then the same weather should give the
same air in any season. The boundary layer is also low on many warm-season
nights. Does the air get dirty then?

```{r fig-same-weather, fig.height=4.8}
season_hours <- city_hourly %>%
  filter(season %in% c("Winter", "Warm season"), !is.na(blh))

blh_breaks <- c(0, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600, Inf)

same_weather <- season_hours %>%
  mutate(blh_class = cut(blh, blh_breaks)) %>%
  group_by(season, blh_class) %>%
  summarise(blh_mid = median(blh), pm25_med = median(pm25),
            q25 = quantile(pm25, 0.25), q75 = quantile(pm25, 0.75),
            n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n >= 50)

ggplot(same_weather, aes(blh_mid, pm25_med, colour = season, fill = season)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q25, ymax = q75), alpha = 0.18, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  who_line() +
  geom_text(data = ~ filter(.x, blh_class == levels(blh_class)[1]),
            aes(label = season), vjust = -1.6, hjust = 0.1, fontface = "bold", size = 3.8) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.05))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = SEASON_COLOURS) + scale_fill_manual(values = SEASON_COLOURS) +
  labs(title = "Under the same lid, winter air is several times dirtier",
       subtitle = "Median hourly PM2.5 at each boundary layer height. Bands show the middle 50% of hours.",
       x = "Boundary layer height (m, log scale)", y = PM_AXIS, caption = SOURCE) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{r same-weather-numbers}
low_lid <- season_hours %>% filter(blh <= 50) %>% group_by(season) %>% summarise(med = median(pm25), n = n())
high_lid <- season_hours %>% filter(blh > 800) %>% group_by(season) %>% summarise(med = median(pm25))
get <- function(tbl, s) tbl$med[tbl$season == s]
```

The two seasons are drawn in one panel on a shared axis, so they can be
compared directly at each lid height. The lines are labelled directly instead
of using a legend. The bands show the spread, not only the middle.

**What we see.** This is the central chart of the project.

- In the warm season the line is flat. Under a lid below 50 m
  (`r comma(low_lid$n[low_lid$season == "Warm season"])` hours) the median is
  `r round(get(low_lid, "Warm season"), 1)` µg/m³, the same as under a high
  lid. **A low lid over a city that is not emitting traps nothing.**
- In winter, the same low lid gives `r round(get(low_lid, "Winter"), 1)` µg/m³:
  about `r round(get(low_lid, "Winter") / get(low_lid, "Warm season"))` times more.
- When the winter air is well mixed (lid above 800 m), winter drops to
  `r round(get(high_lid, "Winter"), 1)` µg/m³, close to the warm-season level.

## What accounts for what

To put numbers on this, we describe each season with its own model of how
PM2.5 responds to weather, and then swap the weather between them. This
answers two "what if" questions: what if the warm season had winter weather,
and what if winter had warm-season weather?

Temperature is left out of these models on purpose. Cold is weather, but it
is also the reason people heat, so it cannot be assigned to one side.

```{r decomposition}
dispersion_formula <- log(pm25) ~ log(blh) + wind + rh + I(rain > 0)

winter_h <- season_hours %>% filter(season == "Winter")
warm_h   <- season_hours %>% filter(season == "Warm season")

winter_response <- lm(dispersion_formula, data = winter_h)   # how winter emissions react to weather
warm_response   <- lm(dispersion_formula, data = warm_h)     # how warm-season emissions react to weather

# Typical level (geometric mean) under each combination of emissions and weather
level <- function(model, weather_data) exp(mean(predict(model, newdata = weather_data)))

scenarios <- tibble(
  emissions = c("Warm season", "Warm season", "Winter", "Winter"),
  weather   = c("warm-season weather", "winter weather", "warm-season weather", "winter weather"),
  pm25      = c(level(warm_response, warm_h),   level(warm_response, winter_h),
                level(winter_response, warm_h), level(winter_response, winter_h)),
  kind      = c("Measured", "What if", "What if", "Measured")
) %>%
  mutate(label = paste0(emissions, " emissions,\n", weather))

s <- setNames(scenarios$pm25, c("warm", "warm_in_winter_weather", "winter_in_warm_weather", "winter"))
```

```{r fig-decomposition, fig.height=3.8}
ggplot(scenarios, aes(pm25, fct_rev(fct_inorder(label)), fill = emissions, alpha = kind)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", pm25)), hjust = -0.25, size = 4, alpha = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = SEASON_COLOURS, guide = "none") +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c("Measured" = 1, "What if" = 0.55), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, s["winter"] * 1.15), expand = expansion(0)) +
  labs(title = "Winter weather alone changes nothing; winter emissions alone double the level",
       subtitle = "Typical hourly PM2.5 (geometric mean) under each combination of emissions and weather.",
       x = PM_AXIS, y = NULL, caption = SOURCE) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

Bars start at zero because the reader compares their lengths. Solid bars are
measured; lighter bars are model-based "what if" values.

**What we see.**

- Give the warm season winter's weather and the level stays at
  `r round(s["warm_in_winter_weather"], 1)` µg/m³ (measured:
  `r round(s["warm"], 1)`). **Weather alone explains none of the gap.**
- Give winter the warm season's weather and the level is still
  `r round(s["winter_in_warm_weather"], 1)` µg/m³, about
  `r round(s["winter_in_warm_weather"] / s["warm"], 1)` times the warm-season
  level. **This part is emissions.**
- Winter's own weather then multiplies this by about
  `r round(s["winter"] / s["winter_in_warm_weather"], 1)`, giving the measured
  `r round(s["winter"], 1)` µg/m³.

So the two causes do not add up, they multiply: winter is roughly
`r round(s["winter_in_warm_weather"] / s["warm"], 1)` (more emissions) ×
`r round(s["winter"] / s["winter_in_warm_weather"], 1)` (worse weather) ≈
`r round(s["winter"] / s["warm"], 1)` times the warm season. Read the other
way round, the message is the same: under winter weather, switching from
warm-season to winter emissions multiplies the level by
`r round(s["winter"] / s["warm_in_winter_weather"], 1)`. Weather is an
amplifier. It needs something to amplify.

# The human rhythm

## A winter day, hour by hour

```{r fig-diurnal, fig.height=6.4}
diurnal <- city_hourly %>%
  filter(season %in% c("Winter", "Warm season")) %>%
  group_by(season, hour) %>%
  summarise(pm25_med = median(pm25), q25 = quantile(pm25, 0.25), q75 = quantile(pm25, 0.75),
            blh_med = median(blh, na.rm = TRUE),   # na.rm: BLH is missing for Jan-Jun 2024 only
            .groups = "drop")

hour_axis <- scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 21, 3), labels = function(h) sprintf("%02d:00", h),
                                expand = expansion(0.01))

p_pm <- ggplot(diurnal, aes(hour, pm25_med, colour = season, fill = season)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q25, ymax = q75), alpha = 0.18, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  who_line() +
  geom_text(data = ~ filter(.x, hour == 14), aes(label = season),
            vjust = -1.1, fontface = "bold", size = 3.8) +
  hour_axis +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.05))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = SEASON_COLOURS) + scale_fill_manual(values = SEASON_COLOURS) +
  labs(title = "Winter pollution has a daily rhythm; the warm season has none",
       subtitle = "Median PM2.5 by hour of day. Bands show the middle 50% of hours.",
       x = NULL, y = PM_AXIS) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_blh <- ggplot(diurnal, aes(hour, blh_med, colour = season)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  hour_axis +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.05)), labels = comma) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = SEASON_COLOURS) +
  labs(subtitle = "Median boundary layer height by hour of day: the lid rises and falls in both seasons.",
       x = "Hour of day (local time)", y = "Boundary layer (m)", caption = SOURCE) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_pm / p_blh + plot_layout(heights = c(2, 1))
```

```{r diurnal-numbers}
winter_profile <- diurnal %>% filter(season == "Winter")
evening_peak <- winter_profile %>% filter(hour >= 17) %>% slice_max(pm25_med, n = 1)
morning_peak <- winter_profile %>% filter(hour %in% 8:14) %>% slice_max(pm25_med, n = 1)
night_low    <- winter_profile %>% slice_min(pm25_med, n = 1)
warm_range   <- diurnal %>% filter(season == "Warm season") %>% pull(pm25_med) %>% range()
```

The two panels share the same x-axis and are stacked, so each hour can be read
straight down from pollution to lid height.

**What we see.**

- Winter has two peaks: in the evening around
  `r sprintf("%02d:00", evening_peak$hour)` (`r round(evening_peak$pm25_med)` µg/m³)
  and in the late morning around `r sprintf("%02d:00", morning_peak$hour)`
  (`r round(morning_peak$pm25_med)` µg/m³). The cleanest hour is
  `r sprintf("%02d:00", night_low$hour)` (`r round(night_low$pm25_med)` µg/m³).
- The lowest winter pollution comes at the end of the night, when the lid is
  at its lowest but the city is asleep. Pollution rises when people get up and
  again when they come home, heat and cook.
- The warm season has the same daily lid cycle, even stronger, yet its line
  stays between `r round(warm_range[1], 1)` and `r round(warm_range[2], 1)` µg/m³
  all day.

The evening peak is helped by the lid closing at sunset, so it is a joint
effect of weather and activity. But the lid closes every evening in the warm
season too, and nothing happens. The rhythm appears only when there are winter
emissions.

## Working days and weekends

```{r fig-weekday, fig.height=4.2}
city_hourly %>%
  filter(season == "Winter") %>%
  group_by(weekday, hour) %>%
  summarise(pm25 = median(pm25), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(hour, fct_rev(weekday), fill = pm25)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "rocket", direction = -1, limits = c(0, NA), name = PM_LEGEND) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 21, 3), labels = function(h) sprintf("%02d:00", h), expand = expansion(0)) +
  labs(title = "The same rhythm seven days a week",
       subtitle = "Median winter PM2.5 for each hour of each weekday.",
       x = "Hour of day (local time)", y = NULL, caption = SOURCE) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "right")
```

```{r weekend-test}
weekend_data <- winter_model_data %>% mutate(residual = resid(weather_model))
weekend_test <- wilcox.test(residual ~ is_weekend, data = weekend_data)
weekend_gap  <- weekend_data %>% group_by(is_weekend) %>% summarise(m = mean(residual))
weekend_ratio <- exp(diff(weekend_gap$m))   # weekend level relative to working days
```

If commuter traffic were the main source, working days should be dirtier than
weekends. To compare them fairly we remove the weather effect first (we compare
the residuals of the weather model) and use a Wilcoxon rank-sum test, which
does not assume normal data.

**What we see.** The evening and late-morning bands run through all seven
rows. After removing weather, weekends are
`r percent(abs(weekend_ratio - 1))` `r if_else(weekend_ratio > 1, "higher", "lower")`
than working days, and the difference is not statistically significant
(p = `r sprintf("%.2f", weekend_test$p.value)`). **Winter pollution does not
follow the working week.** This points to a source that runs every day in
winter and stops in the warm season, which fits residential heating better
than commuter traffic. Our data cannot identify the source directly, so this
is an indication, not proof.


## When the city stops going to work

Weekends are a weak test: many people in Yerevan work on Saturday. A stronger
one is the New Year holiday, `r length(HOLIDAYS)` consecutive non-working days
at the start of January, when offices, schools and building sites close but
homes are still heated, and more people are at home all day.

```{r holiday-data}
mark_holiday <- function(data) {
  data %>% mutate(day_type = if_else(format(date, "%m-%d") %in% HOLIDAYS,
                                     "New Year holiday", "Ordinary winter day"))
}

holiday_hours <- city_hourly %>% filter(season == "Winter") %>% mark_holiday()

# Shape of the day: evening level relative to morning level, on the same day
day_shape <- holiday_hours %>%
  filter(hour %in% c(7, 8, 9, 20, 21, 22, 23)) %>%
  mutate(part = if_else(hour <= 9, "morning", "evening")) %>%
  group_by(date, day_type, part) %>%
  summarise(pm25 = mean(pm25), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = part, values_from = pm25) %>%
  filter(!is.na(morning), !is.na(evening)) %>%
  mutate(ratio = evening / morning)

shape_test <- wilcox.test(ratio ~ day_type, data = day_shape)
shape_median <- day_shape %>% group_by(day_type) %>% summarise(ratio = median(ratio), n = n())
```

```{r fig-holiday, fig.height=4.6}
holiday_hours %>%
  group_by(day_type, hour) %>%
  summarise(pm25 = median(pm25), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(hour, pm25, colour = day_type)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 6.5, xmax = 9.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.45) +
  annotate("text", x = 8, y = 2, label = "morning", size = 3, colour = "grey35") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 19.5, xmax = 23, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.45) +
  annotate("text", x = 21.2, y = 2, label = "evening", size = 3, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  who_line() +
  geom_text(data = ~ filter(.x, hour == 15),
            aes(label = day_type, vjust = if_else(day_type == "New Year holiday", -1.2, 2.0)),
            fontface = "bold", size = 3.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 21, 3), labels = function(h) sprintf("%02d:00", h),
                     expand = expansion(0.01)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.08))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("New Year holiday" = "#7B3294", "Ordinary winter day" = COL_WINTER)) +
  labs(title = "On holidays the morning peak fades, the evening peak grows",
       subtitle = "Median winter PM2.5 by hour of day, holidays against ordinary winter days.",
       x = "Hour of day (local time)", y = PM_AXIS, caption = SOURCE) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Both curves are drawn in one panel on a shared axis so the *shape* can be
compared, not just the level. The two periods used in the test are shaded
(Gestalt principle of enclosure).

**What we see.** The holiday evening is
`r sprintf("%.1f", shape_median$ratio[shape_median$day_type == "New Year holiday"])`
times its own morning, against
`r sprintf("%.1f", shape_median$ratio[shape_median$day_type == "Ordinary winter day"])`
on ordinary days (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p =
`r sprintf("%.4f", shape_test$p.value)`;
`r shape_median$n[shape_median$day_type == "New Year holiday"]` holiday days
against `r shape_median$n[shape_median$day_type == "Ordinary winter day"]`).
Because this is a ratio within the same day, it does not depend on how bad
that day's weather was.

So the two peaks have different owners. The morning peak needs the city to go
to work; it fades when the city stays home. The evening peak does not fade, it
grows, and it grows on days when nobody commutes. The air does not get cleaner
overall during the holidays. Whatever produces most of the winter load keeps
running when the city stops.

# What is burning?

Our sensors show that winter emissions exist, when they appear, and that they
run every day. They cannot tell us *what* is burning. No measured breakdown of
Yerevan's PM2.5 by source has been published, so we bring in two published
datasets that bear directly on the question.

```{r load-heating}
gas_monthly <- read_project_csv(
  "armenia_household_gas_monthly_2020.csv",
  cols(month = col_integer(), gas_mln_kwh = col_double(), source = col_character())
)
heating_fuels <- read_project_csv(
  "yerevan_heating_fuels.csv",
  cols(fuel = col_character(), share_of_households_pct = col_double(),
       pm25_kg_per_tj = col_double(), .default = col_character())
)
```

## Pollution follows the heating calendar

Household gas use is a good record of how much homes are heated in each
month (the flat summer level is cooking and hot water). If heating drives winter pollution, the two calendars should match.

```{r fig-heating-calendar, fig.height=5.6}
heating_calendar <- city_hourly %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(pm25 = median(pm25), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(gas_monthly, by = "month") %>%
  mutate(month_name = factor(month.abb[month], levels = month.abb),
         period = if_else(month %in% WINTER_MONTHS, "Winter", "Rest of the year"))

calendar_cor <- cor(heating_calendar$pm25, heating_calendar$gas_mln_kwh, method = "spearman")

period_fill <- scale_fill_manual(values = c("Winter" = COL_WINTER, "Rest of the year" = "grey75"), guide = "none")

p_cal_pm <- ggplot(heating_calendar, aes(month_name, pm25, fill = period)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) + who_line() + period_fill +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(title = "The air gets dirty in the months when homes are heated",
       subtitle = "Median PM2.5 by month (our sensors, 2023 to 2026)",
       x = NULL, y = PM_AXIS)

p_cal_gas <- ggplot(heating_calendar, aes(month_name, gas_mln_kwh, fill = period)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) + period_fill +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(c(0, 0.05)), labels = comma) +
  labs(subtitle = "Natural gas used by households in Armenia by month (2020)",
       x = NULL, y = "Million kWh",
       caption = paste0(SOURCE, "\nGas use: R2E2 (2022), Analysis of Options for Sustainable Heating in Armenia."))

p_cal_pm / p_cal_gas
```

The two quantities have different units, so they are drawn in two aligned
panels with a shared month axis, not on one chart with two y-axes (a double
axis lets the designer create any impression by rescaling). Bars start at zero.

**What we see.** The two calendars have the same shape: low from May to
October, a jump in November, a peak in December and January. The rank
correlation across the twelve months is `r sprintf("%.2f", calendar_cor)`.
The match is not perfect: from February to April homes are still heated but
the air is already cleaner, because the lid over the city rises in spring.
Heating supplies the particles and weather decides how many stay, as in
Section 6. The gas data is national and from 2020, so it shows the *calendar*
of heating, not its amount in our winters. Gas itself burns cleanly, which leads to the
next question: which heating fuel produces the particles?

## A few stoves can outweigh a city of boilers

A household survey gives the heating fuels of Yerevan homes, and emission
inventories give how much PM2.5 each fuel releases per unit of heat. Combining
the two shows which fuel the heating particles come from.

```{r heating-shares}
heating_shares <- heating_fuels %>%
  mutate(
    heating_share  = share_of_households_pct / sum(share_of_households_pct),   # homes can name several fuels
    particles      = share_of_households_pct * pm25_kg_per_tj,                 # assumes equal heat per home
    particle_share = particles / sum(particles)
  )

wood <- heating_shares %>% filter(fuel == "Firewood")
gas  <- heating_shares %>% filter(fuel == "Natural gas")
```

```{r fig-heating-shares, fig.height=3.6}
heating_shares %>%
  select(fuel, `Share of home heating` = heating_share, `Share of heating particles (PM2.5)` = particle_share) %>%
  pivot_longer(-fuel, names_to = "measure", values_to = "share") %>%
  mutate(measure = fct_rev(fct_inorder(measure))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(share, fct_rev(fct_inorder(fuel)), fill = measure)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, 1)), position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent(), limits = c(0, 1.08), expand = expansion(0)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Share of home heating" = "grey70", "Share of heating particles (PM2.5)" = "grey15"),
                    name = NULL, guide = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  labs(title = "Firewood heats few homes but produces almost all heating particles",
       subtitle = "Yerevan households by heating fuel, and the estimated share of heating PM2.5 from each fuel.",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "Fuel shares: ILCS 2020 household survey (in R2E2, 2022). Emission factors: German emission inventory (2025).") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

For each fuel the two bars sit side by side (Gestalt principle of proximity),
so the eye compares them directly. The values are printed on the bars, so no
gridlines are needed to read them.

**What we see.** Firewood is the heating fuel of about
`r percent(wood$heating_share, 1)` of Yerevan homes, yet it accounts for about
`r percent(wood$particle_share, 1)` of the particles from home heating. The
reason is the emission factor: per unit of heat, burning wood releases about
`r comma(wood$pm25_kg_per_tj / gas$pm25_kg_per_tj)` times more PM2.5 than
burning gas. A city heated mostly by gas can still have a wood-smoke problem.

**How far this goes.** This is an estimate, not a measurement. It assumes the
same heat demand per home, uses emission factors from modern German
appliances (older stoves emit more), and leaves out open burning of leaves and
waste, the wood-heated villages around the city that share the same basin, and
particles that form in the air from boiler and traffic gases. All of these
except the last push in the same direction: towards solid fuel and open
burning as the main winter source. Traffic is not ruled out as a contributor,
but it runs all year, and the warm season shows what traffic alone produces.

# Where, and is it getting worse?

## Across the city

```{r fig-map, fig.width=7, fig.height=5.6}
last_winter <- max(winter_daily$winter)

sensor_winter <- pm %>%
  add_time_parts() %>%
  filter(season == "Winter", winter_label(date) == last_winter) %>%
  group_by(sensor_id) %>%
  summarise(pm25 = median(pm25), n_hours = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(sensors, by = "sensor_id")

ggplot(sensor_winter, aes(lon, lat)) +
  annotate("point", x = 44.5126, y = 40.1777, shape = 3, size = 4, colour = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = 44.5126, y = 40.1777, label = "Republic Square", hjust = -0.12, size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_point(aes(fill = pm25), shape = 21, size = 6, colour = "grey20") +
  geom_label_repel(aes(label = paste0("Sensor ", sensor_id, ": ", round(pm25))),
                   size = 3, box.padding = 0.9, point.padding = 0.6, min.segment.length = 0,
                   label.size = 0.15, seed = 3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "rocket", direction = -1, limits = c(0, NA), name = PM_LEGEND) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(44.44, 44.60), ylim = c(40.12, 40.23)) +
  labs(title = "Polluted everywhere, most of all in the south",
       subtitle = paste0("Median hourly PM2.5 (\u00b5g/m\u00b3) per sensor, winter ", last_winter, ". Each circle is one sensor."),
       x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude", caption = SOURCE) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

The value is encoded by colour, not by circle size, because people judge areas
poorly. `coord_quickmap()` keeps the correct proportion between longitude and
latitude, so distances are not stretched.

**What we see.** Every sensor has a winter median above the WHO guideline,
from `r round(min(sensor_winter$pm25))` to `r round(max(sensor_winter$pm25))` µg/m³.
The highest values are in the south of the city. Two sensors (83131 and 85218)
stand about 200 m apart and report nearly the same value, which again supports
the reliability of the devices. With `r nrow(sensor_winter)` sensors we can
describe differences between these places, not map whole districts.

## Three winters compared

The number of sensors grew over time, which could fake a trend. So here we use
only the two sensors that cover all three winters
(`r paste(LONG_SENSORS, collapse = " and ")`), on days when both reported.

```{r trend}
trend_data <- sensor_daily %>%
  filter(sensor_id %in% LONG_SENSORS) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  filter(n() == length(LONG_SENSORS)) %>%        # days when both sensors are present
  summarise(pm25 = mean(pm25), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(weather_daily, by = "date") %>%
  filter(month(date) %in% WINTER_MONTHS) %>%
  mutate(winter = winter_label(date))

# Ratio of each winter to the first one, with Newey-West confidence intervals
winter_ratios <- function(model, label) {
  ct <- coeftest(model, vcov. = NeweyWest(model))
  rows <- str_detect(rownames(ct), "^winter")
  tibble(winter = str_remove(rownames(ct)[rows], "winter"),
         ratio  = exp(ct[rows, "Estimate"]),
         low    = exp(ct[rows, "Estimate"] - 1.96 * ct[rows, "Std. Error"]),
         high   = exp(ct[rows, "Estimate"] + 1.96 * ct[rows, "Std. Error"]),
         version = label)
}

trend_raw      <- lm(log(pm25) ~ winter, data = trend_data)
trend_adjusted <- lm(log(pm25) ~ winter + wind + temp + rh + rain_day, data = trend_data)

ratios <- bind_rows(winter_ratios(trend_raw, "As measured"),
                    winter_ratios(trend_adjusted, "Adjusted for weather"))
```

```{r fig-trend, fig.height=4.4}
p_box <- ggplot(trend_data, aes(winter, pm25)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = COL_WINTER, alpha = 0.6, outlier.size = 0.7, linewidth = 0.35) +
  who_line() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(subtitle = "Daily PM2.5 per winter", x = NULL, y = PM_AXIS_LOG)

p_ratio <- ggplot(ratios, aes(winter, ratio, colour = version)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), position = position_dodge(width = 0.4),
                  linewidth = 0.8, size = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste(x, "times")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("As measured" = "grey50", "Adjusted for weather" = COL_WINTER), name = NULL) +
  labs(subtitle = "Level relative to winter 2023/24 (95% intervals)", x = NULL, y = "Ratio to 2023/24")

p_box + p_ratio +
  plot_annotation(title = "No sign of improvement over three winters",
                  caption = SOURCE)
```

The adjustment uses wind, temperature, humidity and rain. Boundary layer height
cannot be used here because it is missing for half of the first winter.

```{r trend-numbers}
adj <- ratios %>% filter(version == "Adjusted for weather")
```

**What we see.** After adjusting for weather, the level was
`r percent(adj$ratio[1] - 1)` higher in `r adj$winter[1]` and
`r percent(adj$ratio[2] - 1)` higher in `r adj$winter[2]` than in 2023/24.
The intervals are wide and reach down to "no change" (a ratio of 1), so this
is not proof of a rising trend. What we can say is that the air has not
improved, and that the higher levels of the latest winter are not explained
by worse weather.

# Do the results hold?

We repeat the four headline numbers under different choices. If a conclusion
depended on one choice, it would change here.

```{r robustness}
headline <- function(hourly) {
  daily   <- build_daily(hourly)
  w_daily <- daily %>% filter(season == "Winter", !is.na(blh))
  seasons <- hourly %>% filter(season %in% c("Winter", "Warm season"), !is.na(blh))
  same_weather_model <- lm(log(pm25) ~ log(blh) + wind + rh + I(rain > 0) + season, data = seasons)
  tibble(
    `Winter median PM2.5 (µg/m³)`         = median(hourly$pm25[hourly$season == "Winter"]),
    `Winter days above WHO guideline`     = mean(daily$pm25[daily$season == "Winter"] > WHO_DAILY),
    `Day-to-day variation explained by weather` =
      summary(lm(log(pm25) ~ log(blh) + wind + temp + rh + rain_day, data = w_daily))$r.squared,
    `Winter vs warm season at equal weather` = exp(coef(same_weather_model)[["seasonWinter"]])
  )
}

variants <- list(
  "Main analysis"                       = city_hourly,
  "Without very humid hours (RH > 90%)" = city_hourly %>% filter(is.na(rh) | rh <= HUMID_LIMIT),
  "Only the four long-running sensors"  = build_city_hourly(pm %>% filter(sensor_id %in% PANEL_SENSORS)),
  "Winter 2024/25 and its warm season"  = city_hourly %>% filter(date >= "2024-05-01", date < "2025-05-01"),
  "Winter 2025/26 and its warm season"  = city_hourly %>% filter(date >= "2025-05-01", date < "2026-05-01")
)

robustness <- map_dfr(variants, headline, .id = "Variant")

robustness %>%
  mutate(`Winter median PM2.5 (µg/m³)` = round(`Winter median PM2.5 (µg/m³)`, 1),
         across(c(`Winter days above WHO guideline`, `Day-to-day variation explained by weather`), ~ percent(.x, 1)),
         `Winter vs warm season at equal weather` = paste(round(`Winter vs warm season at equal weather`, 1), "times")) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

Low-cost sensors can over-read in fog, so the second row removes very humid
hours. The last column is the winter-to-warm-season ratio from one model that
holds lid height, wind, humidity and rain equal.

**What we see.** The numbers move, but the conclusions do not: in every
variant most winter days exceed the guideline, weather explains roughly half
of the day-to-day variation, and winter air is at least twice as dirty as
warm-season air under the same weather.

# Limitations

- **Citizen sensors.** They are not reference monitors. Their absolute values
  can be off, but their agreement with each other (Section 4) supports the
  patterns, which is what our argument uses.
- **One weather point.** Weather comes from a reanalysis grid cell for central
  Yerevan, not from a station. It describes city-wide conditions well, local
  ones less so.
- **Few sensors early on.** Until December 2023 only one or two sensors were
  active, so the first winter is less certain.
- **Association, not proof.** We show what weather can and cannot explain. We
  do not measure sources directly. "Heating" is the explanation most
  consistent with the patterns, not a measured fact.
- **Published figures in Section 8.** The fuel survey and gas data are from
  2020 and the emission factors from another country. They indicate the
  likely source; they do not measure it.
- **PM2.5 only.** These sensors report PM10 as well, but the ratio between the
  two is almost constant (about 0.5) in every month and every hour, which is a
  property of this sensor model rather than of the air. PM10 therefore carries
  no information here that PM2.5 does not.
- **"Emissions" is a remainder.** In the season comparison, "emissions" means
  everything that differs between the seasons apart from lid height, wind,
  humidity and rain.
- **Temperature belongs to both sides.** Cold is weather, and cold makes
  people heat. We kept it out of the season comparison for this reason.

# Verdict

**Is it the weather, or is it us? It is both, but not in the same way.**

1. **Weather decides which days are bad.** Lid height and wind explain
   `r percent(weather_r2)` of the day-to-day variation within winter. On this
   point the official explanation is right.
2. **Weather does not create the pollution.** Under the same low lid, warm-season
   air stays at about `r round(get(low_lid, "Warm season"))` µg/m³ and winter
   air reaches `r round(get(low_lid, "Winter"))`. With winter weather but
   warm-season emissions, the city would stay at about
   `r round(s["warm_in_winter_weather"])` µg/m³, far below the WHO guideline.
3. **What accounts for what.** Winter is about `r round(s["winter"] / s["warm"], 1)`
   times dirtier than the warm season: roughly
   `r round(s["winter_in_warm_weather"] / s["warm"], 1)` times from winter emissions
   and `r round(s["winter"] / s["winter_in_warm_weather"], 1)` times from winter
   weather acting on them.
4. **The human fingerprint.** Pollution follows the daily routine of the city,
   runs seven days a week, exists only in the heating season, and has not
   declined over three winters. During the New Year holiday the morning peak
   fades while the evening peak grows, so the main load is not commuting.

5. **What is burning.** Pollution follows the heating calendar. Among heating
   fuels, firewood serves about `r percent(wood$heating_share, 1)` of Yerevan
   homes but produces about `r percent(wood$particle_share, 1)` of heating
   particles. This is an estimate from published figures, not a measurement.

**What the city can do.**

- **Reduce what gets trapped.** The weather cannot be changed, the emissions
  can. The evidence points first at solid-fuel stoves and open burning: few
  households, most of the heating particles. Helping those homes switch to
  clean heating would cut the largest source while affecting the fewest people.
- **Use the forecast, and act early.** Lid height and wind are forecast a day
  ahead. Because pollution accumulates by about
  `r percent(wind_change$pct_per_day[1], 1)` a day once the air goes still, the
  gain from acting on the first calm day is much larger than acting on the
  fourth. Alerts and temporary limits belong at the start of a stagnant spell.
- **Measure sources.** Our data shows *when* and *how much*, not *what burns*.
  A source study would turn this indication into evidence.

# Appendix A: model check {-}

The weather model assumes a roughly linear relationship, constant spread and
roughly normal residuals. The third panel shows how strongly each day's
residual is related to the previous days, which is why we used Newey-West
standard errors.

```{r fig-diagnostics, fig.height=3.4}
diag <- tibble(fitted = fitted(weather_model), residual = resid(weather_model))
acf_values <- acf(diag$residual, lag.max = 14, plot = FALSE)
acf_data <- tibble(lag = as.numeric(acf_values$lag)[-1], acf = as.numeric(acf_values$acf)[-1])
acf_limit <- 1.96 / sqrt(nrow(diag))

p1 <- ggplot(diag, aes(fitted, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1) + geom_smooth(se = FALSE, colour = COL_WHO, linewidth = 0.6) +
  labs(subtitle = "Residuals vs fitted", x = "Fitted log(PM2.5)", y = "Residual")
p2 <- ggplot(diag, aes(sample = residual)) +
  geom_qq(alpha = 0.5, size = 1) + geom_qq_line(colour = COL_WHO) +
  labs(subtitle = "Normal Q-Q plot", x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Residual quantiles")
p3 <- ggplot(acf_data, aes(lag, acf)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5, fill = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-acf_limit, acf_limit), linetype = "dashed", colour = COL_WHO) +
  labs(subtitle = "Autocorrelation of residuals", x = "Lag (days)", y = "Correlation")

p1 + p2 + p3
```

# Appendix B: the design rules we followed {-}

The course gives rules for honest and readable charts. The table says where
each one is used. "Lie Factor" is Tufte's ratio between the size of an effect
as drawn and its size in the data; it should be 1.

```{r principles-table}
tribble(
  ~Figure,                      ~`Chart type`,            ~`Principles applied`,
  "Three years of daily PM2.5", "Line + shaded bands",    "Zero origin; winters grouped by enclosure; WHO line gives context (compared to what?); events labelled on the plot",
  "Calendar of bad days",       "Heatmap",                "Sequential palette, dark = more; classes set at WHO health thresholds; gridlines removed (data-ink)",
  "Seasonal gap",               "Boxplots, log scale",    "Whole distributions, not means; log scale because the data is right-skewed; share above guideline printed",
  "Sensor agreement",           "Correlation heatmap",    "Lower triangle only (the rest is redundant ink); scale fixed to 0-1 so high values are not exaggerated; square cells",
  "Lid and wind",               "Binned heatmap",         "Binning instead of thousands of overplotted points; minimum group size; sequential palette",
  "Weather effects",            "Coefficient plot",       "Uncertainty shown as intervals; effects converted to percent change so the units are readable",
  "Episodes build and break",   "Bars + change bars",     "Bars from zero; change drawn around a zero line with the two directions in two colours",
  "The longest episode",        "Stacked panels",         "Shared x-axis so days align (proximity); the episode marked by enclosure",
  "Same weather, different air","Two lines + bands",      "Direct labels instead of a legend (similarity, connection); shared axis for a fair comparison; spread shown, not only the middle",
  "What accounts for what",     "Bars",                   "Zero origin; measured and modelled values separated by transparency, not by colour",
  "Daily rhythm",               "Line + ribbon, stacked", "Uncertainty as an interquartile band; the lid panel aligned below so hours can be read down",
  "Holiday test",               "Two lines",              "Compared by shape on one axis; the two tested periods marked by enclosure",
  "Heating calendar",           "Two aligned bar panels", "Two y-axes avoided: a double axis can be rescaled to suggest any relationship",
  "Heating fuels",              "Paired bars",            "Pairs placed side by side (proximity); values printed so no gridlines are needed",
  "Sensor map",                 "Points on coordinates",  "Value shown by colour, not by area, because areas are judged poorly; map proportions kept correct",
  "Three winters",              "Boxplots + intervals",   "Raw and adjusted shown together; intervals included so the reader sees what is uncertain"
) %>% knitr::kable()
```

Colour is used in one way throughout: a qualitative pair for the two seasons
(different in both hue and lightness, so it survives greyscale and the common
forms of colour blindness), sequential scales for amounts, and diverging scales
centred on zero where zero is meaningful. Every chart carries its units and its
source. No chart uses 3D, a second y-axis, or a rainbow palette.
```{r session}
sessionInfo()
```
